title: I'm going to, I intend to
why: The near future (הוֹלֵךְ לְ־ + infinitive), very common in speech, and the words for saying what you intend to do, what you're planning, and what you'd like. With them, you can invite someone, and accept or decline politely.

{"lessons": ["

I'm going to buy: הוֹלֵךְ לְ־

Good news: Hebrew works just like English. \"I'm going to buy\" uses the verb \"to go,\" הוֹלֵךְ, followed by the infinitive in לְ־ / לִ־.

FormHebrewPronunciation
m. sg.הוֹלֵךְholekh
f. sg.הוֹלֶכֶתholekhet
m. pl.הוֹלְכִיםholkhim
f. pl.הוֹלְכוֹתholkhot
אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לִקְנוֹת לֶחֶם.I'm going to buy bread. [ani holekh liknot lekhem]
הִיא הוֹלֶכֶת לִלְמֹד בְּחֵיפָה.She's going to study in Haifa. [hi holekhet lilmod be-Kheifa]
אֲנַחְנוּ הוֹלְכִים לִרְאוֹת סֶרֶט.We're going to see a movie. [anakhnu holkhim lir'ot seret]

הוֹלֵךְ לִכְתֹּב (I'm going to write) announces an action that's coming soon or already decided; אֶכְתֹּב (I will write) is the simple future.

The trap: הוֹלֵךְ agrees with the subject, but the infinitive never changes: הִיא הוֹלֶכֶת לִקְנוֹת, הֵם הוֹלְכִים לִקְנוֹת.

", "

Intentions and wishes

Two verbs for talking about your plans. They agree like all present-tense forms, in gender and number:

Formto intendto plan
m. sg.מִתְכַּוֵּן mitkavenמְתַכְנֵן metakhnen
f. sg.מִתְכַּוֶּנֶת mitkavenetמְתַכְנֶנֶת metakhnenet
m. pl.מִתְכַּוְּנִים mitkavnimמְתַכְנְנִים metakhnenim
f. pl.מִתְכַּוְּנוֹת mitkavnotמְתַכְנְנוֹת metakhnenot
אֲנִי מִתְכַּוֶּנֶת לִלְמֹד עִבְרִית.I intend to learn Hebrew (a woman is speaking). [ani mitkavenet lilmod ivrit]
הֵם מְתַכְנְנִים טִיּוּל לְאֵילַת.They're planning a trip to Eilat. [hem metakhnenim tiyul le-Eilat]

מִתְכַּוֵּן is followed by an infinitive with לְ־; מְתַכְנֵן can be followed by an infinitive or a noun.

For a polite wish: הָיִיתִי רוֹצֶה (a man) / הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה (a woman), \"I would like.\" Word for word: \"I was wanting.\" It's a conditional form (\"would\"), which you'll study later; for now, learn it as a set phrase.

אֲנִי רוֹצֶה = I want; הָיִיתִי רוֹצֶה = I would like, softer and more polite.

", "

Inviting, accepting, declining

To find out whether someone is free, you use the present: מָה אַתָּה עוֹשֶׂה הָעֶרֶב? (to a man) / מָה אַתְּ עוֹשָׂה הָעֶרֶב? (to a woman), \"what are you doing tonight?\"

In speech, people often drop the pronoun in an invitation:

רוֹצֶה לָבוֹא אִתִּי לַקּוֹלְנוֹעַ?Do you want to come to the movies with me? (to a man) [rotse lavo iti la-kolno'a?]
רוֹצָה לָבוֹא אִתִּי לַקּוֹלְנוֹעַ?Do you want to come to the movies with me? (to a woman) [rotsa lavo iti la-kolno'a?]

To accept: בְּשִׂמְחָה! (with pleasure!) or סַבָּבָה! (sure, great!). To decline nicely: חֲבָל, אֲנִי לֹא יָכוֹל (a man) / אֲנִי לֹא יְכוֹלָה (a woman), אוּלַי בַּפַּעַם הַבָּאָה (maybe next time).

The article plays the role of \"this\": הַיּוֹם (today, \"this day\"), הָעֶרֶב (this evening, tonight). But בָּעֶרֶב means \"in the evening.\"
